question: Can a physics-encoded recurrent convolutional surrogate reconstruct derivatives well enough from coarse noisy grids that conventional sparse regression and coefficient fine-tuning recover the governing nonlinear PDE?

key_findings.claim: The proposed discovery workflow is a three-stage composition of high-resolution reconstruction, sparse library selection, and coefficient-only recurrent fine-tuning.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 1 and Sections 3.2-3.4 first fit a PeRCNN to low-resolution measurements, use its dense rollout to form a candidate library and run STRidge, then freeze the selected PDE structure and optimize its scalar coefficients against all measurements. The stages reduce noisy numerical differentiation and separate term selection from coefficient refinement, but the final result remains conditional on the reconstruction and sparse-support decisions made upstream.

key_findings.claim: PeRCNN hard-codes useful physical structure, but the paper presents an antecedent architecture as a novel contribution without cleanly separating the new discovery wrapper from prior work.
key_findings.evidence: The recurrent update follows forward Euler, circular padding enforces periodic boundaries, a frozen finite-difference convolution supplies a known diffusion term, and a multiplicative Pi-block represents polynomial interactions. Yet the same authors' arXiv:2106.04781v1 already introduced PeRCNN, its Pi-block, hard physics encoding, reconstruction studies, and Burgers interpretability; this paper cites that work on page 12, and arXiv explicitly flags substantial text overlap. The defensible new contribution is therefore the particular PeRCNN-STRidge-fine-tuning pipeline and its experiments, not the reconstruction architecture itself.

key_findings.claim: Appendix A's 'universal polynomial approximator' language is broader than the argument supports.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix reproduces a finite-difference filter lemma and observes that products of convolution outputs can form monomials. This supports representation of bounded-degree polynomial combinations of state variables and approximable spatial derivatives when filter size, moments, degree, and time step are adequate. It does not prove universal approximation of arbitrary nonlinear functions, nor that an unconstrained learned filter is an identifiable derivative. With n parallel factors the degree is capped at n, and page 19 concedes that derivative filters must be frozen or moment-constrained to extract the genuine PDE form.

key_findings.claim: Under the paper's strongest shared 10% Gaussian-noise condition, the method exactly recovers both Burgers supports but not both Lambda-Omega or Gray-Scott supports.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 reports Burgers relative coefficient error 0.59% with 100% precision and recall; Lambda-Omega 5.44% with 91.6% precision and 100% recall; and Gray-Scott 10.03% with 85.7% precision and recall. These are markedly better than the displayed baselines, but only Burgers has exact support. Equations 6-8 show close coefficients at the selected conditions. The table contains one result per condition, with no repeated seeds, variability, or significance test.

key_findings.claim: Robustness depends strongly on the interaction between spatial resolution, pattern scale, and noise; it is not a general 30%-noise guarantee.
key_findings.evidence: Table E.1 shows that at 30% Gaussian noise Burgers retains 100% recall but only 75% precision and 9.10% coefficient error, Lambda-Omega retains 100% recall and 91.6% precision with 15.89% error, while Gray-Scott collapses to 33.3% precision, 37.5% recall, and 238.31% error. The authors correctly attribute the last failure to its 26x26 grid and fine maze-like patterns and state a noise-sparsity tradeoff.

key_findings.claim: The experiments study coarse regular grids rather than genuinely few irregular measurements, and all data are generated by numerical solvers for equations already used to design the priors and libraries.
key_findings.evidence: Burgers and Lambda-Omega use 40 snapshots on 51x51 grids, while Gray-Scott uses 160 snapshots on a 26x26 grid—roughly 104,000 to 108,000 scalar grid-time observations per state before reconstruction. Every dataset is synthetic, periodic, and produced with high-order finite differences and Runge-Kutta integration. Appendix F considers fixed grids down to 11x11; at that resolution Lambda-Omega reaches only 90.9% precision and 83.3% recall, while Gray-Scott requires at least 26x26. The evidence does not cover scattered sensors, missing regions, non-Gaussian noise, or experimental measurements.

key_findings.claim: The baseline comparison does not isolate the value of the complete pipeline under matched priors, tuning, and implementations.
key_findings.evidence: The proposed model is given known diffusion, periodic boundaries, and a polynomial structural prior; the diffusion coefficient is protected from sparse thresholding. FCNN+SR is explicitly denied the known-diffusion prior. The PDE-Net baseline is an author adaptation that replaces the Pi-block in their own recurrent model with a delta-t block, not a direct run of the published method. The paper also says PDE-Net's additive form can learn only linear PDEs, whereas the cited PDE-Net describes neural approximation of nonlinear responses. There is no component-matched comparison that gives every reconstructor the same physics, derivative estimator, library, tuning budget, and coefficient-refinement stage.

key_findings.claim: Support selection and interpretability still require substantial human and structural intervention.
key_findings.evidence: The candidate libraries are hand-built to contain the true polynomial and derivative terms; diffusion is assumed known and exempted from filtering; Gray-Scott receives an additional literature-derived polynomial-reaction assumption. Appendix H says the Pareto front may be unclear and choosing the sparsity weight remains 'more art than science.' Appendix J obtains an interpretable Burgers expression only after manually freezing derivative filters, and the extracted Equation 13 still contains expanded nuisance constants rather than the compact true law.

anchors.section: Section 4.4, Burgers library and known diffusion

key_findings.claim: The public repository is a useful but non-reproducing partial artifact whose hard-coded scripts diverge from the paper protocol.
key_findings.evidence: Repository commit 6e27b4559b11d6b92b2d8be1d282b1bd86731b74 contains syntactically valid Python scripts and some checkpoints for Burgers and Lambda-Omega, plus external data links. It omits Gray-Scott, a dependency lock, tests, CI, a license, raw table outputs, and a complete scripted workflow; code forces CUDA. All four Stage-2 scripts sample 20% of rows although page 6 says 10%. The Burgers Stage-1 script uses 10,000 iterations rather than the 15,000 stated on page 7 and starts with restart=True from a checkpoint. Several Stage-2 input filenames are hard-coded to 20% or 30% noise, and the nominal Burgers 5%-noise Stage-3 script actually calls add_noise with 0.0. Thus the published numbers were not independently rerunnable from the snapshot without editing code and reconstructing undocumented choices.

method.core_idea: Use a recurrent finite-difference-shaped neural surrogate to denoise and super-resolve coarse PDE trajectories, then recover a sparse equation from the surrogate rollout and refit only the selected coefficients against the original measurements.
method.mechanism: An initial-state generator upsamples the first measurement. A recurrent Pi-block advances the state with a forward-Euler residual update; parallel convolutions followed by elementwise products represent polynomial interactions, while frozen finite-difference highway filters insert known diffusion and circular padding enforces periodic boundaries. Training minimizes low-resolution rollout error plus an initial-state regularizer. The dense rollout supplies temporal and spatial derivatives for a hand-built candidate matrix. STRidge searches a coefficient threshold under an error-plus-l0 objective, using a manually selected Pareto weight. Finally, a recurrent block containing only the selected PDE terms refits coefficients on all observed grid-time points.
assumptions: The governing dynamics are local, Markovian, autonomous PDEs representable by the chosen state variables and derivative order.
The right-hand side is sparse in a manually supplied candidate library that contains every true term.
A bounded-degree polynomial in states and spatial derivatives is an adequate form for the unknown nonlinear dynamics.
Known diffusion terms, periodic boundary conditions, and other encoded priors are correct and do not exclude the true equation.
The fixed regular grid and temporal sampling resolve the smallest physically relevant structures after learned reconstruction.
Forward-Euler recurrence with the chosen internal time step remains numerically stable over the trained rollout.
The PeRCNN reconstruction is accurate enough that finite-difference derivatives of its rollout preserve the correct sparse support.
Gaussian noise scaled to each field's standard deviation represents the measurement corruption of interest.
Randomly selected library rows and the STRidge train-test split are representative despite spatial and temporal dependence.
Manual Pareto selection of the l0 weight is stable and does not use knowledge of the ground-truth support.
Once support is selected, coefficient-only recurrent fine-tuning does not compensate for a structurally wrong equation.
Synthetic solver trajectories with fixed parameters are representative of the experimental discovery setting claimed in motivation.

techniques.role: Shapes the surrogate as an explicit time-step update rather than an unconstrained space-time regressor.
Multiplies parallel convolution features to represent polynomial products of states and spatial derivatives.
Injects a known Laplacian term through a frozen finite-difference convolution and protects it during support selection.
Hard-encodes periodic boundary conditions in every convolutional recurrent update.
Learns a high-resolution initial state from the first coarse measurement before recurrent rollout.
Computes candidate derivatives from the denoised dense rollout rather than directly from noisy coarse observations.
Uses sequential threshold ridge regression to select a sparse support from a predefined PDE library.
Balances library residual and support size by manually selecting an error-complexity tradeoff weight.
Rebuilds a recurrent solver from the selected terms and optimizes only their scalar coefficients on all measurements.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic 2D Burgers, Lambda-Omega reaction-diffusion, and Gray-Scott reaction-diffusion trajectories on periodic regular grids with 0%, 5%, or 10% additive Gaussian noise
evaluations.metric: Relative l2 coefficient error, support precision, and support recall
evaluations.result: At 10% noise, the proposed method reports 0.59% / 100% / 100% on Burgers, 5.44% / 91.6% / 100% on Lambda-Omega, and 10.03% / 85.7% / 85.7% on Gray-Scott. It is best in nearly every Table 1 cell, but the table reports no repetition or uncertainty and only Burgers has exact support at the hardest shared condition.
evaluations.baseline: PDE-FIND, FCNN plus sparse regression, and an author-adapted PDE-Net plus sparse regression

evaluations.setting: Additional Gaussian-noise sweep from 0% through 30% on all three synthetic systems
evaluations.metric: Relative l2 coefficient error, support precision, and support recall
evaluations.result: Burgers and Lambda-Omega degrade moderately through 30% noise, but Gray-Scott falls to 238.31% coefficient error, 33.3% precision, and 37.5% recall at 30%. This demonstrates a resolution-pattern-noise tradeoff rather than uniform high-noise robustness.
evaluations.baseline: Lower-noise runs of the same proposed pipeline

evaluations.setting: Spatial-grid sparsity sweep for Lambda-Omega and Gray-Scott
evaluations.metric: Support precision and recall at 51x51, 26x26, 21x21, and 11x11 resolutions
evaluations.result: Gray-Scott requires at least 26x26 for discovery because of its fine pattern; Lambda-Omega at 11x11 retains 90.9% precision and 83.3% recall. The appendix gives selected endpoint results but no full numeric table or uncertainty.
evaluations.baseline: Different spatial resolutions of the same method

evaluations.setting: Component studies for known diffusion and coefficient fine-tuning
evaluations.metric: Training/validation loss curves and coefficient error before versus after fine-tuning
evaluations.result: The frozen diffusion highway converges faster and ends with lower reconstruction loss in Figure D.1. Fine-tuning reduces every displayed coefficient error: for example Burgers at 10% noise falls from 2.18% to 0.59%, while Gray-Scott falls from 12.33% to 10.03%. No repeated-run variance or ablation of the complete three-stage pipeline is reported.
evaluations.baseline: PeRCNN without encoded diffusion and sparse-regression coefficients before fine-tuning

evaluations.setting: Higher-Reynolds Burgers case with viscosity 0.002, Reynolds number 500, and 10% Gaussian noise
evaluations.metric: Qualitative reconstructed snapshot and recovered equation coefficients
evaluations.result: Equation 12 recovers diffusion near 0.002 and advection coefficients within roughly 1% of unity. It is one synthetic trajectory with no comparator, repeats, rollout metric, or support table.

evaluations.setting: Public code audit at commit 6e27b4559b11d6b92b2d8be1d282b1bd86731b74, checked 2026-08-24
evaluations.metric: Coverage, dependency and data lineage, executable workflow, protocol correspondence, tests, licensing, and retained outputs
evaluations.result: All 12 Python files parse, and the repository retains partial checkpoints and links to data, but only Burgers and Lambda-Omega are represented. There is no locked environment, test suite, CI, license, raw result bundle, or one-command workflow; CUDA is mandatory. Hard-coded sample fractions, iterations, noise filenames, and one 5%-labeled script's zero-noise call diverge from the paper, so the headline table was not reproduced.
evaluations.baseline: Exact ICLR/arXiv protocol and the three systems reported in Table 1

limitations: Author-acknowledged (p.15-16): tolerable noise depends on spatial resolution and pattern scale; Gray-Scott discovery deteriorates sharply at 20-30% noise.
Author-acknowledged (p.17): coefficient fine-tuning is dependent on sparse regression and cannot repair a wrong support, as seen for Lambda-Omega and Gray-Scott at 10% noise.
Author-acknowledged (p.17): the sparsity-error Pareto front can be ambiguous, so selecting the regularization weight remains manual and problem-dependent.
Author-acknowledged (p.19): interpretable derivative terms require chosen filters to be frozen or moment-constrained; unconstrained Pi-block weights do not automatically identify genuine operators.

Reviewer-identified: the fixed-depth Pi-block represents only a bounded-degree polynomial family, so the universal-approximator label does not cover arbitrary nonlinear, nonlocal, fractional, delayed, or rational PDE terms.

Reviewer-identified: the PeRCNN architecture, hard encoding, and Burgers interpretability experiment substantially derive from the authors' earlier arXiv:2106.04781; the manuscript and arXiv metadata do not sharply delimit that lineage.

Reviewer-identified: all measurements are synthetic solver outputs with known periodic boundaries and known diffusion; no laboratory, field, irregular-sensor, missing-region, or non-Gaussian data are evaluated.
Reviewer-identified: roughly 10^5 grid-time observations per state is coarse relative to the reconstructed tensor but not a few-measurement regime in absolute terms.

Reviewer-identified: candidate libraries and physical priors are target-informed, so the search does not test missing terms, wrong boundary conditions, unknown derivative order, or misleading domain knowledge.
Reviewer-identified: a single result per condition, without error bars, repeated seeds, support frequencies, or significance tests, cannot establish optimizer stability.

Reviewer-identified: the proposed model and baselines receive unequal physical priors and architectural treatment, and the PDE-Net comparator is an author reimplementation rather than the published method.

Reviewer-identified: hyperparameters are selected with a 10% holdout from the same synthetic trajectory, but the split geometry, leakage control, and matched baseline tuning budgets are not described.

Reviewer-identified: temporal-spatial rows randomly subsampled for STRidge are highly dependent, making its internal train-test score an optimistic model-selection signal rather than independent generalization evidence.

Reviewer-identified: the claim that the three stages can iterate until convergence has no algorithm, stopping rule, iteration study, or corresponding released workflow; reported experiments appear to use one pass.

Reviewer-identified: no runtime, hardware, memory, number of trainable parameters, or cost-normalized comparison is reported despite 15,000-step recurrent training and repeated high-resolution rollout.
Reviewer-identified: the public artifact is partial and protocol-divergent, omitting Gray-Scott, dependency pins, tests, CI, a license, raw table outputs, and direct reproduction commands.
failure_modes: A true term absent from the candidate library can never be recovered, while a correlated nuisance term can replace it with low residual.
Incorrect known diffusion or boundary conditions are hard-coded into every rollout and protected from sparse elimination, biasing the recovered law.
Fine-scale structures lost by coarse sampling cannot be reconstructed uniquely; Gray-Scott's high-noise collapse illustrates this information limit.
Reconstruction error can create systematic derivative bias that sparse regression interprets as new PDE terms.
Forward-Euler rollout can become unstable or overly dissipative when the learned dynamics are stiff or the internal time step is too large.
Products of learned convolution features are non-identifiable: many filters and factorizations can yield the same polynomial, obstructing physical interpretation.
Manual Pareto selection can exploit visual knowledge of the target support or choose different equations under small perturbations.
A wrong sparse support survives coefficient fine-tuning because the final recurrent network optimizes magnitudes but cannot add omitted terms.
Random row splits leak neighboring space-time information and can understate sparse-regression generalization error.
Gaussian-noise scaling omits bias, drift, missing sensors, correlated noise, outliers, and discretization mismatch common in experiments.
A target-informed polynomial library can make synthetic discovery appear automatic while concealing the combinatorial problem of choosing operators in a new domain.
The released scripts require manual edits, external data, CUDA, and condition-specific file naming; executing them as checked can silently run a different noise or subsampling protocol.
reusable_insights: Denoise and reconstruct before differentiating when raw finite differences amplify measurement noise, but audit derivative bias independently from field error.
Use hard physical constraints for knowledge that is genuinely certain and soft or testable alternatives for assumptions that may be wrong.
Separate support discovery from coefficient refinement; a lower-dimensional final fit can improve coefficients substantially once support is correct.
Report support precision and recall alongside coefficient error because large coefficients can hide omitted small but essential terms.
Vary spatial resolution and noise jointly; neither robustness dimension is meaningful without the pattern length scale.
Distinguish relative scarcity from absolute observation count and report sensors, snapshots, scalar values, and reconstruction ratio separately.
Give every baseline the same physical priors, derivative library, tuning budget, and coefficient-refinement opportunity when isolating the reconstruction model.
Use grouped trajectory or region splits for model selection rather than random space-time rows that share local dynamics.
Treat an explicit neural expression as physical only after canonicalization, operator-identifiability checks, and validation under new initial and boundary conditions.
Automate the sparsity path and publish every Pareto candidate so manual support selection remains auditable.
Store condition-specific configuration rather than encoding noise, grid size, and checkpoint behavior in filenames and source constants.
Make paper tables rebuild from immutable raw outputs and a locked environment; partial code release is not equivalent to result reproduction.
open_questions: How much of the gain remains when PeRCNN, FCNN, PDE-Net, and weak-form methods receive identical known diffusion and boundary priors?
Can reconstruction uncertainty be propagated into derivative estimates and sparse support probabilities rather than producing one deterministic equation?
What recovery conditions link coarse sampling, feature length scale, noise, and candidate-library coherence for this three-stage estimator?
Can weak-form differentiation replace dense neural reconstruction while retaining robustness and reducing compute?
How should the method detect that the candidate library, boundary condition, or known physics is wrong before returning a confident equation?
Does alternating the three stages actually converge, and can a support change after coefficient fine-tuning improve rather than destabilize discovery?
Would blocked cross-validation or multiple independent trajectories select the same sparsity weight as the manual Pareto procedure?
Can the Pi-block support non-polynomial, nonlocal, fractional, parametric, and spatially heterogeneous dynamics without losing interpretability?
How stable are discovered supports and coefficients over seeds, sensor layouts, solver discretizations, and realistic correlated noise?
Do equations learned from sparse experimental measurements predict interventions, new parameters, and new boundary conditions better than black-box surrogates?
Which exact released configuration and checkpoints produced every Table 1 and Appendix E result, and can the missing Gray-Scott workflow be reconstructed?

competitive_landscape.title: Data-driven discovery of partial differential equations
competitive_landscape.difference: PDE-FIND directly estimates derivatives, constructs a candidate library, and selects sparse terms with STRidge and Pareto analysis. The target paper retains that discovery engine but inserts learned high-resolution reconstruction before it and coefficient recurrent fine-tuning after it, trading more priors and computation for noise tolerance.

competitive_landscape.title: PDE-Net: Learning PDEs from Data
competitive_landscape.difference: PDE-Net jointly learns constrained convolutional differential operators and nonlinear responses for prediction and discovery. PeRCNN hard-encodes selected operators and uses multiplicative features before a separate sparse regression stage; the paper's comparator is an adapted delta-t block inside its own recurrent scaffold rather than a direct PDE-Net reproduction.

competitive_landscape.title: Physics-informed learning of governing equations from scarce data
competitive_landscape.difference: PiDL combines a continuous neural field, automatic differentiation, physics residuals, and sparse regression and includes experimental as well as numerical studies. The target paper replaces the continuous black-box field with a hard-encoded discrete recurrent surrogate, making known grid physics explicit but restricting geometry and time stepping.

competitive_landscape.title: Weak SINDy: Galerkin-Based Data-Driven Model Selection
competitive_landscape.difference: WSINDy avoids pointwise noisy derivatives by integrating against test functions and supplies favorable coefficient-error scaling under white noise. The target paper instead learns a dense surrogate before standard differentiation; it can exploit hard physics but is computationally heavier and introduces reconstruction bias.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v3, 2020-07-03; Journal of Computational Physics 2021

competitive_landscape.title: PDE-READ: Human-readable Partial Differential Equation Discovery using Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: PDE-READ uses rational networks to learn the response and hidden PDE, followed by parameter-free sparse extraction, and tests six equations with open-source software. PeRCNN uses a stronger fixed-grid physics encoding and conventional STRidge with manual Pareto tuning, but evaluates fewer systems and requires more prior structure.

competitive_landscape.title: Encoding physics to learn reaction-diffusion processes
competitive_landscape.difference: This earlier PeRCNN work establishes the product block, hard finite-difference and boundary encoding, reconstruction, generalization, and interpretability used by the target. The ICLR paper's incremental contribution is the explicit three-stage coupling to STRidge and coefficient fine-tuning, not a new recurrent architecture.

competitive_landscape.title: Physics-Guided Discovery of Highly Nonlinear Parametric Partial Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: This method incorporates observational constraints and basic physical laws to discover PDEs with highly nonlinear spatially varying coefficients, including three-dimensional cases, and provides an error-reduction analysis. The target focuses on constant-coefficient polynomial 2D systems and uses physics mainly to reconstruct a clean grid before sparse selection.

competitive_landscape.title: Automating the Discovery of Partial Differential Equations in Dynamical Systems
competitive_landscape.difference: ARGOS-RAL automates differentiation, library construction, and recurrent adaptive-lasso selection and tests noise, sample size, nonuniform sampling, and pure-noise rejection. The target gains robustness through a physics-encoded neural reconstructor but leaves library design and Pareto support selection substantially manual.

competitive_landscape.title: PhysPDE: Rethinking PDE Discovery and a Physical Hypothesis Selection Benchmark
competitive_landscape.difference: PhysPDE reframes discovery as selecting and fitting interpretable physical hypotheses through nonlinear mixed-integer optimization and evaluates fluid-mechanics and laser-fusion tasks. The target searches a generic polynomial-derivative library on three canonical simulations, offering cleaner coefficients but weaker physical-hypothesis and benchmark coverage.

competitive_landscape.title: Unrolled-SINDy: A Stable Explicit Method for Non linear PDE Discovery from Sparsely Sampled Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Unrolled-SINDy explicitly decouples numerical integration step size from the observation interval and works with both closed-form and gradient-based fitting, targeting sparse temporal sampling without requiring dense learned super-resolution. PeRCNN reconstructs a dense grid first and can inject more spatial physics, but does not analyze sampling-step bias.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper presents a novel physics-encoded discrete-learning framework and recurrent architecture that reconstruct high-resolution dynamics from scarce noisy measurements, discover a sparse PDE, and fine-tune its coefficients while rigorously respecting known physics.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The manuscript assembles forward-Euler recurrence, a multiplicative convolutional Pi-block, frozen known-physics filters, encoded periodic boundaries, learned initial-state upscaling, STRidge support selection, Pareto sparsity tuning, and coefficient-only recurrent refinement. Across three synthetic 2D systems it reports substantially better support and coefficient metrics than three adapted baselines, and appendices explore known diffusion, noise, resolution, fine-tuning, higher Reynolds number, and interpretation.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The three-stage composition and demonstration that PeRCNN reconstruction can feed sparse PDE discovery are useful incremental contributions. The central reconstruction architecture, hard-physics mechanisms, polynomial product block, and Burgers interpretation are inherited from the authors' earlier PeRCNN work, as confirmed by source comparison and arXiv's overlap notice. STRidge, Pareto selection, finite-difference libraries, and coefficient refinement also have clear antecedents. The universal-approximation phrasing is overstated, and the empirical contribution is a controlled synthetic proof of concept under target-informed priors rather than a general solution to scarce-data PDE discovery. Later weak-form, parameter-free, parametric, automated, physical-hypothesis, and unrolled methods broaden the relevant comparison substantially.

Inspection covered Figures 1-2, D.1, H.1, and I.1; Tables 1, C.1, E.1, G.1, and H.1; Equations 1-13; Lemma 1 and its proof; references; and Appendices A-J. The current official arXiv record has one revision and explicitly notes substantial text overlap with arXiv:2106.04781; exact v1 source archive SHA-256 is d388534f8e55c25abd9a567f409199c1ac6ba84249e720df0d585d0611ef66a8. Source comparison used the antecedent arXiv:2106.04781v1 archive SHA-256 4c0a5b62927d6e924388b3a33a31c2a8abe097489d84968dd19b94a61c164339. Artifact audit used author repository commit 6e27b4559b11d6b92b2d8be1d282b1bd86731b74 on 2026-08-24; its Python files were syntax-compiled, but GPU training and paper results were not rerun because the repository lacks a locked environment, a complete workflow, and all reported conditions.
